title: Bur-Sagale solar eclipse recorded in Assyrian eponym list
note: The eclipse noted in the eponym year of Bur-Sagale anchors the whole Assyrian chronology and, through it, the dates of the Israelite and Judean kings.

title: Epoch of the Era of Nabonassar
note: Ptolemy counted his astronomical era from noon on this day, the first of Thoth in the accession year of the Babylonian king Nabonassar.

title: Lunar eclipse observed at Babylon (oldest in the Almagest)
note: A total lunar eclipse seen from Babylon in the first year of Merodach-baladan II, which Ptolemy preserved as his earliest dated observation.

title: Total solar eclipse described by Archilochus
note: The poet wrote that Zeus made night at midday; this total eclipse over the Aegean is the most likely match.

title: Nabopolassar recognized as king of Babylon
note: Nabopolassar formally took the throne after driving out the Assyrians, founding the Neo-Babylonian dynasty.

title: Nebuchadnezzar II takes the throne of Babylon
note: Fresh from Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar hurried back to Babylon after his father died and was enthroned on 1 Ululu.

title: Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem and deposes Jehoiachin
note: The Babylonian Chronicle dates the surrender of Jerusalem to 2 Addaru of Nebuchadnezzar's seventh year.

title: Eclipse of Thales halts the Lydian-Median battle
note: Herodotus says a battle at the Halys ended when day became night; this is the only solar eclipse that fits, though the identification is debated.

title: Death of Nebuchadnezzar II
note: Babylonian business documents show Nebuchadnezzar died in early October after a reign of 43 years, succeeded by Amel-Marduk (Evil-merodach).

title: Babylon falls to the Persian army of Cyrus
note: According to the Nabonidus Chronicle, Gobryas entered Babylon without battle on 16 Tashritu, ending the Neo-Babylonian empire.

title: Cyrus the Great enters Babylon
note: Cyrus arrived seventeen days after his troops took the city and proclaimed peace to its people.

title: Gaumata (false Bardiya) rises in revolt
note: The Behistun inscription dates the start of the magus's uprising to 14 Viyaxana.

title: Gaumata seizes the Persian kingship
note: Behistun says the pretender took the kingdom on 9 Garmapada, after Cambyses had died.

title: Darius and the Six kill Gaumata
note: Darius and his fellow nobles killed the usurper in a Median fortress on 10 Bagayadi and Darius became king.

title: Darius defeats Nidintu-Bel on the Tigris
note: Darius forced the river crossing against the Babylonian rebel who styled himself Nebuchadnezzar III.

title: Darius defeats Nidintu-Bel again at Zazana
note: Five days after the Tigris crossing, Darius won a second victory on the Euphrates and moved on to take Babylon.

title: Solar eclipse recalled in Pindar's ninth Paean
note: A near-total eclipse at Thebes is the most probable event behind Pindar's poem on the darkened sun.

title: Solar eclipse in the first summer of the Peloponnesian War
note: Thucydides notes that the sun became crescent-shaped and some stars appeared, at a new moon in the war's first year.

title: Partial solar eclipse noted by Thucydides
note: Thucydides records a small eclipse at the start of the eighth year of the war.

title: Lunar eclipse delays the Athenian retreat from Syracuse
note: Nicias put off the withdrawal for weeks after the eclipse, and the Athenian expedition was then destroyed.

title: Lunar eclipse before Gaugamela
note: The Babylonian astronomical diary records this total eclipse, which unsettled Darius III's army eleven days before the battle.

title: Alexander defeats Darius III at Gaugamela
note: Dated by a Babylonian astronomical diary, the battle opened Babylon and the Persian heartland to Alexander.

title: Death of Alexander the Great at Babylon
note: A Babylonian astronomical diary says "the king died" in the Babylonian day running from the evening of 10 June to the evening of 11 June.
source: Wikipedia: Death of Alexander the Great

title: Total solar eclipse seen by Agathocles' fleet
note: The day after the tyrant of Syracuse slipped past the Carthaginian blockade on his way to invade Africa, his fleet saw the sun totally eclipsed.

title: Priests' synod issues the Decree of Canopus
note: The trilingual decree honouring Ptolemy III tried to add a leap day to the Egyptian civil calendar every four years.

title: Death of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of China
note: The first emperor died while touring at Shaqiu; his ministers hid the death to manoeuvre Huhai onto the throne.

title: Liu Bang crowned emperor, founding the Han dynasty
note: After defeating Xiang Yu, Liu Bang took the title of emperor on the jiawu day of the second month.

title: Memphis decree of the Rosetta Stone
note: The priests assembled at Memphis for the coronation anniversary of Ptolemy V and passed the decree later carved on the Rosetta Stone.

title: Death of Emperor Gaozu of Han (Liu Bang)
note: The founder of the Han died at Chang'an, leaving Empress Lü as the real power behind his young son.

title: Emperor Wen of Han takes the throne
note: Once the Lü clan had been purged, court officials brought Liu Heng from Dai and enthroned him.

title: Lunar eclipse recorded at Alexandria
note: One of the Hellenistic observations Ptolemy used to work out the motion of the Moon.

title: Lunar eclipse on the eve of Pydna
note: The tribune Sulpicius Gallus is said to have explained the eclipse to the Roman troops beforehand; it fixes the battle's Julian date.

title: Rome defeats Perseus of Macedon at Pydna
note: Aemilius Paullus' victory ended the Antigonid kingdom; the eclipse shows the Roman calendar was then running months ahead of the seasons.

title: Death of Emperor Wen of Han
note: Emperor Wen, remembered for his frugal and lenient rule, died at Chang'an.

title: Emperor Wu of Han ascends the throne
note: Liu Che became emperor at fifteen and went on to the longest and most expansive reign of the Western Han.

title: Death of Emperor Wu of Han
note: After 54 years on the throne Emperor Wu died, having pushed Han power into Central Asia and Korea.

title: Julian calendar comes into force
note: Caesar's reformed solar calendar began after the 445-day "year of confusion"; whether the first day was Julian 1 or 2 January depends on how the early leap years are reconstructed.

title: Caesar defeats the Pompeians at Munda
note: Munda was the last battle of Caesar's civil war, fought in southern Spain against Pompey's sons.

title: Julius Caesar assassinated on the Ides of March
note: Senators led by Brutus and Cassius stabbed the dictator at a meeting of the Senate in the Theatre of Pompey.

title: First battle of Philippi
note: Antony beat Cassius, who killed himself thinking the day was lost, while Brutus overran Octavian's camp.

title: Second battle of Philippi; Brutus defeated
note: The triumvirs' victory destroyed the Liberators' cause, and Brutus took his own life.

title: Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at Actium
note: Agrippa's fleet won the naval battle off western Greece that left Octavian master of the Roman world.

title: Senate confers the name Augustus on Octavian
note: Three days after Octavian made a show of handing back his powers, the Senate gave him the name by which the first emperor is known.

title: Partial lunar eclipse often linked to Herod's death
note: Josephus mentions a lunar eclipse shortly before Herod the Great died, and this one is the usual choice of chronologists; the eclipse date is exact, the link is debated.

title: Death of Augustus at Nola
note: The first emperor died in Campania after 41 years as sole ruler; the month Sextilis already bore his name.

title: Senate recognizes Tiberius as emperor
note: The Senate meeting that deified Augustus also confirmed Tiberius, under whom the ministry of Jesus took place.

title: Lunar eclipse calms the Pannonian mutiny
note: Tacitus tells how mutinous legionaries took the eclipse as an omen, which helped Drusus restore order.

title: Wang Mang killed as rebels take Chang'an
note: The usurper of the short-lived Xin dynasty was killed after rebels broke into the capital.

title: Liu Xiu proclaims himself Emperor Guangwu, restoring the Han
note: His proclamation began the Eastern Han dynasty, which later moved its capital to Luoyang.

title: Death of Tiberius
note: Tiberius died at Misenum and was succeeded by Caligula.

title: Caligula assassinated; Claudius proclaimed
note: Praetorian officers killed Caligula on the Palatine, and the guard acclaimed his uncle Claudius the same day.

title: Death of Claudius; Nero becomes emperor
note: Claudius, who had expelled the Jews from Rome, died (reportedly poisoned) and his stepson Nero succeeded him.

title: Death of Emperor Guangwu of Han
note: The restorer of the Han died at Luoyang after more than thirty years on the throne.

title: Great Fire of Rome breaks out
note: Tacitus dates the start of the fire to 19 July; Nero blamed the Christians, beginning the first persecution.

title: Suicide of Nero
note: Declared a public enemy by the Senate, Nero killed himself outside Rome, ending the Julio-Claudian line.

title: Galba murdered; Otho becomes emperor
note: The praetorians killed Galba in the Forum and acclaimed Otho in the Year of the Four Emperors.

title: Suicide of Otho after Bedriacum
note: Otho killed himself after his army lost to the Vitellians in northern Italy.

title: Vespasian proclaimed emperor at Alexandria
note: The legions in Egypt hailed Vespasian, then commanding the Jewish War, as emperor; he later counted his reign from this day.

title: Vitellius killed as Flavian troops take Rome
note: Vespasian's supporters stormed the city and lynched Vitellius, leaving Vespasian sole emperor.

title: Total solar eclipse described by Plutarch
note: Plutarch's description of a total eclipse that began near noon, with stars visible, is usually matched to this one.

title: Death of Vespasian
note: The emperor who began the Colosseum died, and his son Titus, who had destroyed Jerusalem, succeeded him.

title: Death of Titus
note: Titus died after a short reign marked by the eruption of Vesuvius; his brother Domitian took the throne.

title: Domitian assassinated; Nerva becomes emperor
note: Court officials murdered Domitian, whose reign Christian tradition remembers for persecution, and the Senate chose Nerva.

title: Death of Nerva; Trajan succeeds
note: Nerva died after adopting Trajan, the first emperor from the provinces.

title: Hadrian announces his accession
note: Word of Trajan's death and his adoption reached Hadrian at Antioch.

title: Death of Hadrian
note: The emperor who crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt and refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina died at Baiae.

title: Death of Antoninus Pius
note: Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus succeeded as joint emperors.

title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
note: The philosopher-emperor died on campaign on the Danube and Commodus succeeded him.

title: Commodus strangled
note: A palace conspiracy killed Commodus, opening the Year of the Five Emperors.

title: Pertinax murdered; the empire is auctioned
note: Praetorians killed Pertinax and then sold the throne to Didius Julianus.

title: Death of Septimius Severus at York
note: Severus died in Britain, leaving the empire to his sons Caracalla and Geta.

title: Geta murdered on Caracalla's orders
note: Caracalla had his brother killed, reportedly in their mother's arms.

title: Caracalla assassinated near Carrhae
note: A soldier killed Caracalla on the road to Carrhae, and the praetorian prefect Macrinus took power.

title: Death of Cao Cao
note: The warlord who had dominated northern China died at Luoyang; his son Cao Pi inherited his position.

title: Emperor Xian abdicates to Cao Pi, ending the Han
note: The last Han emperor handed over the throne, ending four centuries of Han rule and opening the Three Kingdoms era.

title: Cao Pi proclaims himself emperor of Wei
note: Cao Pi formally took the imperial title and founded the state of Cao Wei.

title: Liu Bei becomes emperor of Shu Han
note: Claiming to carry on the Han line, Liu Bei took the throne at Chengdu.

title: Death of Liu Bei at Baidicheng
note: Liu Bei died after his defeat by Wu, leaving the regency to Zhuge Liang.

title: Ardashir defeats Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan
note: Artabanus died in the battle, ending Parthian rule and beginning the Sasanian empire.

title: Sun Quan declares himself emperor of Wu
note: With this proclamation all three of the Three Kingdoms had their own emperor.

title: Death of Sun Quan
note: The founding emperor of Eastern Wu died at Jianye after a long rule.

title: Pope Sixtus II martyred in the catacombs
note: Sixtus and several deacons were executed under Valerian's edict against clergy; Lawrence followed days later.

title: Cyprian of Carthage beheaded
note: The proconsular record of the bishop's trial survives, and he was executed the same day.

title: Sima Yan proclaims the Jin dynasty
note: Four days after forcing the last Wei emperor to abdicate, Sima Yan took the throne as Emperor Wu of Jin.

title: Sun Hao surrenders, reuniting China under Jin
note: The fall of Wu ended the Three Kingdoms period.

title: Diocletian acclaimed emperor at Nicomedia
note: The army chose Diocletian after Numerian died; the Coptic Era of the Martyrs is counted from his reign.

title: Death of Emperor Wu of Jin
note: His death led to the succession of the incapable Emperor Hui and soon to the War of the Eight Princes.

title: Church at Nicomedia razed on the Terminalia
note: Diocletian chose the festival of the boundary god Terminus to begin the Great Persecution.

title: First edict of the Great Persecution published
note: The edict ordered scriptures burned, churches destroyed, and Christians stripped of legal privileges.

title: Diocletian and Maximian abdicate
note: The two senior emperors retired on the same day and handed power to Galerius and Constantius.

title: Constantius dies; Constantine acclaimed at York
note: The troops at York hailed Constantine as emperor on the day his father died.

title: Galerius' edict of toleration published
note: Lactantius says the dying Galerius' edict ending the persecution was posted at Nicomedia on the day before the Kalends of May.

title: Constantine defeats Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge
note: Constantine, who credited the Christian God with his victory, became master of the West.
source: Wikipedia: Battle of the Milvian Bridge

title: Licinius' letter on religious freedom posted at Nicomedia
note: The rescript, known as the Edict of Milan, gave back confiscated church property and granted freedom of worship.

title: Constantine defeats Licinius at Chrysopolis
note: The victory made Constantine sole emperor of the Roman world.

title: First Council of Nicaea convenes
note: Socrates gives the opening date of the first ecumenical council, which condemned Arius; some scholars put it in June.

title: Constantinople dedicated as the new capital
note: Constantine formally inaugurated his refounded city on the Bosporus.
source: OUP blog: This Day in World History

title: Annular solar eclipse recorded by Firmicus Maternus
note: The astrologer Firmicus, who later wrote a Christian polemic against paganism, mentions this eclipse in his Mathesis.
source: Wikipedia: List of solar eclipses in antiquity

title: Death of Constantine after deathbed baptism
note: Eusebius of Nicomedia baptized Constantine shortly before he died near Nicomedia.

title: Constantius II defeats Magnentius at Mursa
note: One of the bloodiest battles of the century, which badly weakened Roman manpower.

title: Death of Constantius II; Julian sole emperor
note: Constantius died marching against his rebel cousin Julian, who then openly returned to paganism.

title: Death of Julian the Apostate in Persia
note: The last pagan emperor died of a wound taken in battle during his retreat from Ctesiphon.

title: Death of Athanasius of Alexandria
note: The great defender of Nicene doctrine died in Alexandria after five exiles.

title: Ambrose consecrated bishop of Milan
note: Acclaimed bishop while still an unbaptized governor, Ambrose was baptized and consecrated within a week.

title: Death of Valentinian I
note: The emperor reportedly died of a stroke while raging at Quadi envoys.

title: Goths destroy the Roman army at Adrianople
note: Emperor Valens was killed in the worst Roman defeat in centuries.

title: Theodosius I made emperor of the East
note: Gratian raised Theodosius to rule the East after the disaster at Adrianople.

title: Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state faith
note: Theodosius, Gratian and Valentinian II ordered all their subjects to follow the faith of the bishops of Rome and Alexandria.

title: Battle of the Frigidus begins
note: Over two days Theodosius defeated the usurper Eugenius, who was backed by the last pagan party.

title: Death of Theodosius I; empire divided
note: The last emperor to rule both halves died at Milan, leaving East to Arcadius and West to Honorius.

title: Death of Ambrose of Milan
note: The bishop who baptized Augustine and stood up to Theodosius died on Holy Saturday.

title: Death of John Chrysostom in exile
note: The deposed archbishop of Constantinople died at Comana while being moved to a harsher exile.

title: Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome
note: The Goths came in through the Salarian Gate, and the shock led Augustine to write The City of God.

title: Death of Augustine of Hippo
note: Augustine died while the Vandals were besieging Hippo.

title: Council of Ephesus opens under Cyril
note: Cyril of Alexandria opened the third ecumenical council before the Antiochene bishops arrived; it deposed Nestorius.

title: Leo the Great elected bishop of Rome
note: Leo was chosen in his absence while on a diplomatic mission in Gaul.

title: Council of Chalcedon opens
note: The fourth ecumenical council defined Christ as one person in two natures.

title: Valentinian III assassinated
note: Retainers of the murdered general Aetius killed the emperor, ending the Theodosian dynasty in the West.

title: Death of Pope Leo the Great
note: Leo, whose Tome shaped Chalcedon and who met Attila, died after 21 years as pope.

title: Total lunar eclipse recorded by Hydatius
note: The Galician bishop-chronicler recorded the eclipse in his chronicle of the barbarian invasions.

title: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus
note: The deposition of the last western emperor is traditionally taken as the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

title: Death of Julius Nepos in Dalmatia
note: Nepos was murdered in Dalmatia; he was the last western emperor still recognized by Constantinople.

title: Second Temple burned by the Romans
note: Titus's army burned the Temple on the Ninth of Av, fulfilling Jesus' word that not one stone would be left on another (Matt. 24:2). The day follows Ken Johnson's Ninth-of-Av table (4 August); Josephus gives the 10th of Lous, usually reckoned 30 August (Julian).
source: Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8; Ken Johnson, Ancient Prophecies Revealed (Ninth of Av)
